NASA Runs Competition To Help Make Old Fortran Code Faster

If I know Voat, there's going to be a stream of comments saying that this is "government waste" or proof of obsolescence, and questions as to why we are still using fortran, why we aren't rewriting. Let me just throw in my two cents as a programmer and hardware designer who has dealt with quite a few of the older languages out of curiosity.

There are two paradigms to programming: Procedural and Object Oriented. Back in FORTRAN's heyday, however, Object Oriented programming hadn't been conceived of yet, so FORTRAN is exclusively procedural. For those who HAVEN'T taken a CS course, You can think of a procedural program being a stream of commands flowing through the computer telling it to perform operations on data, and object oriented as writing code that represents objects, and their behavior (for instance, a car object would store data about itself, say its color and its current speed, along with code relating to its behavior, such as a routine to accelerate). Why Object oriented has been the rage for developing large scale software for years now (and not without reason, if you need to write a big project, OO scales MUCH better), it does have its shortcomings, especially if used when not needed. Primarily, the "Flow of execution" of an object oriented program is considerably harder to follow, especially at scale. This is fine most of the time, you don't need to know the means by which the program got the result it did, simply that the result is correct. What OO is probably least suited for, however, is financial programs. There's not a whole lot of reason to need object representations when manipulating numbers (as the process to add one to the integer 9 is no different than the process to add one to the integer 23. No need to store routines specific to 9, or anything other than its value and a nice label for when it changes and becomes something other than 9), and if you make the order of calculations easier to follow, the odds of there being bugs that result in slight miscalculations decreases dramatically. For this reason, ever since the popularization of object oriented programming, a set of languages has been maintained that are focused around procedural code have been in use. Originally this was legacy fortran code, the majority of which was replaced by cobol, which is now being replaced by R, and to a lesser extent python. For the complex calculations nasa wants, such a "business language" is the right choice. So, while outdated, fortran IS a valid choice, though not one that would be picked for a new project.

So, why are they not rewriting it? In the era when this software was originally written, most of the experts in the field now known as computer science were trained as mathematicians, as the field of computer science wasn't a field one could dedicate a degree to yet, so, for what its worth, the original code is going to be just about as mathematically simple and correct as you can get (because, while programmers take quite a bit of math today, few can crunch numbers like an applied mathematics PHD can), and it's already been pretty exhaustively tested by decades of usage by nasa. Rewriting, ESPECIALLY from a language like fortran, which will not be the most fluent language for any programmer working on the project, is likely to introduce errors that were not previously there. There's no reason to abandon a system that works, when the consequences of fucking up could cost millions of dollars or tens of human lives. (for this reason, there's a language from the 80s, used for designing hardware, VHDL, still in use today. To it's benefit, there was an update to the language in 1992, and another in 2008. The 2008 version of the language remains adopted, as its new, untested, and the hardware this code is used to design runs all kinds of things, such as plane navigation systems. If there's a subtle bug in the language itself, and it manifests itself for the first time in the cockpit of a 747, there's a problem). Should it be rewritten from scratch eventually? Sure, and a project should probably be made to do so, but right now, it makes more sense to improve what works. When such a rewrite IS finished, it will need to be run in parallel with the old code for an extended period of time ANYWAYS, to ensure that its outputs PERFECTLY match the outputs of the old system, so even if it was completed tomorrow, the need for speed improvements for the existing code is still present.
